253.skill_description: Continuously record the target behavior throughout the observation stage, count each occurrence once, and calculate the total number of occurrences to quantify the behavior frequency. It is required to be able to identify the start and end of each occurrence of the behavior.
253.when_to_use: In the behavior observation and recording stage, when planning to use continuous recording to establish or evaluate the baseline, it is necessary to quantify the number of occurrences within the unit phase.
253.trigger: The target behavior can occur multiple times in the observation situation with clear start and end, and observers can distinguish and count its occurrences one by one.

254.skill_description: In continuous recording, timing the total duration from the occurrence to the disappearance of the target behavior, used to measure duration. The beginning and end of the behavior must be clearly definable.
254.when_to_use: Used in the observation stage when the behavior's persistence or time-consuming features need assessing, and continuous recording is used to establish a baseline and change curve.
254.trigger: The start and end of the target behavior can be clearly observed, and its duration is meaningful for assessment, making it easy to record with timing tools.

255.skill_description: In continuous recording, using measuring tools or rating scales to assess the energy intensity contained in the target behavior, to quantify intensity. Suitable for situations where frequency and duration hardly reflect differences in force.
255.when_to_use: When establishing a baseline or tracking, changes in the intensity of the behavior need to be captured rather than only counts or duration, when continuous recording is planned.
255.trigger: The strength of the target behavior differs markedly or is important, and can be graded with instruments or scales.

256.skill_description: In continuous recording, records the length of time from a specific stimulus event to the start of the target behavior, to quantify the latency period, reflecting response delay.
256.when_to_use: When assessing the stimulus-response relationship or training response speed, when a latency baseline needs to be established and continuous recording used.
256.trigger: There is a clear antecedent stimulus or task prompt, and the start time of the target behavior can be precisely recorded.

257.skill_name: Use permanent-product recording to assess behavioral output
257.skill_description: When behavior produces observable outcomes, indirectly evaluating the behavior level by counting these outcomes; the observer need not be present when the behavior occurs.
257.when_to_use: When it is hard to observe on site, but behavior leaves clear results (homework, works, completion amounts) and a quantified baseline and change are needed.
257.trigger: The output of the target behavior can be objectively counted or examined, and the occurrence of the behavior can be inferred from the post-hoc result.

258.skill_description: Dividing the observation period into consecutive short intervals, observing and recording in each interval whether the target behavior occurred, without needing to identify the specific start and end, saving time and effort.
258.when_to_use: When a representative sample needs to be quickly obtained and whether behavior occurs in each interval judged in order to establish a baseline.
258.trigger: The observation plan has divided time intervals, and only needs to judge 'occurred/not yet occurred', not requiring precise start-end information.

259.skill_description: Dividing the observation period into short intervals, recording as occurred only when the target behavior continues throughout the entire interval; if it appears only part of the time, it is recorded as not yet occurred.
259.when_to_use: When focusing on whether the behavior spans the entire interval and a more conservative occurrence criterion is needed to establish a baseline or conduct evaluation.
259.trigger: The observation stage has been divided into time intervals, and the criterion requires the behavior to span the entire interval to count as occurring.

260.skill_name: Implement time-sample recording and calculate percentages
260.skill_description: Divide the observation phase into several intervals, observe only during part of each interval, and finally express the level as the percentage of intervals in which the behavior was recorded out of the total number of intervals.
260.when_to_use: When continuous full observation is impossible, needing to estimate the behavior level by sampling and quantify it as a percentage of intervals.
260.trigger: The observation plan specifies observing only during part of each interval, and the number of intervals in which it occurred and the total number of intervals can be counted.

221.skill_name: Manipulating behavioral consequences to test function
221.skill_description: Directly manipulate the behavioral consequences of the target behavior, systematically monitor the environmental conditions, and observe the impact of changes in consequences such as reinforcement or escape on the problem behavior, so as to test the hypothesis of the maintaining function and identify causal relationships.
221.when_to_use: In the functional assessment stage, used when the causal relationship between maintaining consequences and problem behavior needs to be clarified, or when investigation and direct observation only suggest correlation rather than causation.
221.trigger: The target behavior shows correlational cues with consequences such as gaining attention, gaining items, or escaping demands, but with no causal evidence yet; the frequency of the behavior appears to change systematically after such consequences.

222.skill_name: Manipulate antecedent variables to test effects
222.skill_description: Systematically change antecedent conditions such as task difficulty, task length, attention levels in activities, and opportunities for activity choice, observe the systematic change of the target behavior with changes in the independent variables, so as to explore and confirm its functional effect.
222.when_to_use: When it is suspected that a specific antecedent situation or task feature influences the problem behavior, and experimental manipulation is needed to confirm its causal relationship with the target behavior.
222.trigger: Observational signs of regular increases or decreases in the target behavior under different task difficulties/lengths or attention/choice conditions, suggesting antecedent conditions may affect the behavior.

223.skill_name: Controlling extraneous variables to reduce interference
223.skill_description: Beyond manipulating the independent variable, identifying and controlling other environmental factors that may affect the participant's behavior (extraneous variables), preventing them from interacting with the independent variable to interfere with results, ensuring the validity of causal inference.
223.when_to_use: During the implementation of the experimental method, when potential interfering factors need to be controlled simultaneously to ensure the attributability of the manipulation effect and the accuracy of the experimental conclusions.
223.trigger: Apart from the manipulated variable, there are signs that other environmental factors changed at the same time and the target behavior fluctuated accordingly, affecting interpretation of the results.

224.skill_name: Introducing and withdrawing contrasts to verify causality
224.skill_description: Systematically compare the existence and removal of the independent variable: if introducing the independent variable draws the dependent variable (the target behavior) to change, and the change vanishes after removal, the causal relation between the two can accordingly be determined.
224.when_to_use: When a change in the target behavior has been observed after manipulation, and a reversibility test is needed to further confirm the causal link between the independent variable and the behavior change.
224.trigger: When the target behavior changes consistently upon application of the manipulation, the researcher needs to judge whether that change disappears accordingly after the manipulation is withdrawn, in order to complete the verification.

225.skill_name: Implemented by trained personnel with manipulation supervised throughout
225.skill_description: Considering that the experimental method is precise but highly difficult to implement, assign personnel who have received professional training to carry out the experimental manipulations, and during implementation systematically supervise and control the environment and the behavior, safeguarding methodological quality and safety.
225.when_to_use: When deciding to adopt the experimental method to clarify the causal relationship between environmental events and problem behavior, needing to ensure high-quality implementation and controllable risk.
225.trigger: The assessment shows the problem is complex and experimental confirmation is needed; on-site manipulation involves multi-link control and high technical requirements, so professional personnel and supervision procedures must be arranged.

237.skill_name: Use active verbs to objectively describe visible behavior
237.skill_description: Use active verbs to clearly and objectively describe concrete, visible, recordable behaviors, avoiding vague statements, making them easy to observe, count, and record later as target behaviors, emphasizing the concrete actions and situational elements of behavior occurrence.
237.when_to_use: In the early stage of behavioral observation and recording, when defining target behaviors is needed to formulate a recording plan or clarify the change object before intervention.
237.trigger: The client describes the problem in general or abstract terms, such as 'always disobedient' or 'often not doing things well', lacking specific visible actions and contexts.

238.skill_name: Excluding internal speculation and subjective evaluation
238.skill_description: When defining the target behavior, exclude speculation and value judgments about inner psychological states, express it only based on observable manifestations, avoiding taking feelings and thoughts as definitional content.
238.when_to_use: Before clarifying the target behavior in words or formulating assessment indicators, when it is necessary to ensure the definition is based only on observable behavior.
238.trigger: The client describes the problem in terms of inner states such as 'feeling frustrated' or 'inner resistance', or evaluative wording with value coloring appears.

239.skill_name: Avoid categorical labels; use specific behavioral definitions instead
239.skill_description: Do not name goals with categorical labels such as 'rebellious' or 'social impairment'; instead express them with specific, observable actions or reactions, ensuring meaning does not deviate across different individuals.
239.when_to_use: When forming goal names and definitions, to prevent ambiguity and recording difficulties caused by categorical vocabulary, needing to specify behavioral descriptions.
239.trigger: The client or records use categorical labels such as 'depression', 'procrastination', 'introverted personality', which cannot be directly used for observational recording.

240.skill_name: Establish operational definitions to ensure observational consistency
240.skill_description: Giving the target behavior an operational definition, clarifying start-end criteria, observable indicators and recording rules, so that different observers independently recording obtain consistent conclusions.
240.when_to_use: Before deploying observation records with multiple sessions or multiple observers, when it is necessary to ensure that the target behavior can be recorded repeatedly and consistently across observers.
240.trigger: Different observers are inconsistent in behavioral recording, or disagree during trial recording on behavior start-end points or whether to count.

241.skill_name: Sets goals together with the help-seeker (therapist-led)
241.skill_description: When defining the target behavior, using a collaborative approach led by the therapist with the help-seeker's participation, jointly confirming the specific behavior to be changed, enhancing motivation and reaching agreement.
241.when_to_use: Used after completing the preliminary functional analysis, upon entering the goal setting and definition stage, when a goal definition recognized by both parties needs to be formed.
241.trigger: The client expresses willingness to change or cooperate with assessment, and can participate in discussing the direction and scope of specific behavior change.

242.skill_name: Translate the help-seeker's expectations into observable goals
242.skill_description: Translating the help-seeker's vague expectations into observable, recordable goal statements, defining specific actions, frequencies or contexts, to align evaluation with intervention.
242.when_to_use: Used when, in goal discussion, the client raises a general wish or outcome expectation that needs to be concretized into operable behavioral indicators.
242.trigger: The client says generalized expectations such as 'want to get better', 'hope the relationship improves', lacking observable behavioral standards and situational definitions.

243.skill_name: Goals specific with room for adjustment retained
243.skill_description: Expressing the goal as concretely as possible (such as frequency, duration, situation), while retaining reasonable adjustment room, so that the definition can be revised as needed as data accumulate.
243.when_to_use: Used when first defining goals and available data are limited, when indicators need to be clarified while allowing the definition to be optimized based on subsequent observation.
243.trigger: The client or observer is unsure about target boundaries, or the initial indicators are too rigid to fit real scenarios.

244.skill_name: Refine process goals and discuss them item by item
244.skill_description: Unfold process goals item by item, clarifying steps, criteria, and transition conditions, so that each process link can be observed and recorded, facilitating tracking and feedback.
244.when_to_use: When the goal involves skill acquisition or a gradual change process, needing to break the outcome into monitorable process indicators.
244.trigger: The client's goal is process-oriented phrasing such as 'gradually adapt/learn/practice', with stage behavioral criteria not yet clarified.

245.skill_name: Clarify the client's responsibility for the goals
245.skill_description: When confirming the goal, clarifying the client's responsibility and commitment, agreeing on self-monitoring or cooperation requirements, prompting them to take the main responsibility for executing and feeding back on the goal.
245.when_to_use: When goal definition is complete and the implementation and record-preparation stage begins, and cooperation matters and responsibility boundaries need to be put in place.
245.trigger: The client is vague about implementation and cooperation or externalizes responsibility, needing to clarify responsibility through commitment and division of labor.

168.skill_name: Identifying the sensory positive reinforcement function
168.skill_description: Judging whether the reinforcing consequence comes from internal sensations rather than others, identifying whether the behavior is maintained by self-stimulation; noting manifestations that occur frequently even without others' attention, aimed at obtaining specific sensations.
168.when_to_use: In the initial stage of functional analysis, used to distinguish the functional type of problem behavior, screening whether it is maintained by sensory positive reinforcement.
168.trigger: The individual repeatedly scratches to obtain tingling pleasure, repeatedly throws objects to hear sounds; still occurs at high frequency without others' attention, and they say they 'like that feeling'.

169.skill_name: Use the functional assessment observation form to mark self-stimulation
169.skill_description: In the observation form's 'perceived behavioral function' column checking 'gaining-self-stimulation', simultaneously recording antecedent events and real consequences, examining consistency across different time periods and contexts to verify the hypothesis.
169.when_to_use: The direct observation stage, when functional hypotheses formed by indirect investigation need to be clarified or functional clues systematically collected in natural settings.
169.trigger: Records show the behavior repeatedly occurring at specific times without external attention or item gains; the 'self-stimulation' pattern in the form gradually becomes consistent.

170.skill_name: Verify the sensory function by experimentally manipulating behavioral consequences
170.skill_description: Using experimental methods to systematically manipulate the consequences or related independent variables of the target behavior, observing whether the problem behavior changes systematically accordingly, to clarify whether it is maintained by sensory positive reinforcement.
170.when_to_use: When observational data only indicate correlation without establishing causality, needing to precisely confirm the function before formulating a plan.
170.trigger: Observational data conclusions are inconsistent or hard to interpret; behavior-consequence relationships are vague across different scenarios, affecting functional judgment and plan selection.

171.skill_name: Changing behavior that produces sensory consequences to extinguish self-stimulation
171.skill_description: If the conclusion shows the behavior is maintained by self-stimulation, in the plan directly change the behavior characteristics or conditions that can produce sensory consequences, so that the sensory return decreases, thereby prompting the self-stimulatory behavior to fade.
171.when_to_use: At the stage of establishing the behavior treatment plan, when the functional assessment has clarified self-stimulation as the maintaining factor and the sensory consequences need to be adjusted in the plan.
171.trigger: The conclusive statement points to 'maintained by self-stimulation'; the problem behavior persists even under attention deprivation, suggesting the need to directly weaken the sensory consequence.

172.skill_name: Establishing functionally equivalent alternative behaviors and optimizing reinforcement balance
172.skill_description: Based on the functional-equivalence principle, teaching alternative behaviors that provide acceptable sensory consequences, and ensuring the reinforcement provided for appropriate behavior is not less than what the problem behavior can obtain, to reduce relapse.
172.when_to_use: In the intervention design and implementation stage, when after weakening self-stimulation a functionally equivalent alternative needs to be provided with sufficient reinforcement to maintain the new behavior.
172.trigger: The individual shows a clear preference for specific sensations; simply suppressing the problem behavior causes discomfort or rebound; alternative behavior begins to increase after reinforcement is enhanced.

152.skill_description: In the 'real behavioral consequences' column of the functional assessment observation form, record each time whether, after the problem behavior, others' attention or specific items or activities were obtained, so as to capture the pattern maintained by others' positive reinforcement.
152.when_to_use: In the direct-observation stage of functional assessment, using the functional assessment observation form to collect event-level data, judging whether the problem behavior is maintained by others' attention or giving.
152.trigger: When after each problem behavior, parents/teachers immediately look over, talk, soothe, criticize, or provide toys, phones, snacks, privileges, etc.

153.skill_description: In the observation form's 'perceived behavioral function' column, based on each event checking 'gaining' and specifically marking 'gaining attention/specific items or activities', to form a working hypothesis of socially-mediated positive reinforcement.
153.when_to_use: At the moment of recording each incident, when a preliminary judgment of function is needed and a working hypothesis is formed.
153.trigger: When records show that the consequences are mostly gaining others' attention, items, or activities, rather than leaving the task or escaping demands.

154.skill_name: Preset and record antecedent events such as 'lack of attention'
154.skill_description: In the 'antecedent events' column pre-listing and checking potential indicators such as 'lack of attention', recording whether the behavior was long unattended before occurring, to test the 'lack of attention -> behavior -> gaining attention' functional chain.
154.when_to_use: When formulating and executing observation plans, needing to identify and record the antecedent events of problem behavior to construct the ABC chain.
154.trigger: When signs are observed such as the person being alone and neglected, sparse interaction, interrupted activities, or insufficient situational stimulation.

155.skill_name: Compare the consistency between felt function and real consequences
155.skill_description: Based on the form's interpretation principles, comparing the 'perceived function' with the 'real behavioral consequence' for the same event; if both consistently show gaining attention/items, reinforcing the socially-mediated positive reinforcement conclusion; if inconsistent, revising it.
155.when_to_use: When periodically reviewing observation data, interpreting materials, and writing or revising conclusive statements.
155.trigger: When multiple records appear, but the initial 'gaining' judgment does not match actual consequences or fluctuates unstably across contexts.

156.skill_name: Interviews focus on concrete descriptions of others' reactions
156.skill_description: Using survey methods to interview the person and important others, requiring them to specifically describe others' reactions after the behavior occurred, avoiding subjective inference, focusing on antecedents and consequences, to determine whether others' positive reinforcement maintains the behavior.
156.when_to_use: In the indirect-investigation stage of early functional analysis, or when direct-observation data are insufficient and supplementary clues are needed.
156.trigger: When the interviewee says things involving attention / giving, such as 'when he cries I attend to him' or 'when she makes a fuss the teacher always comes over'.

157.skill_name: Scheduling sufficient observation to confirm relationships
157.skill_description: Select times and places with high incidence of problem behavior for multi-day observation until the relationship between the behavior and the social consequences is clear; usually collect 15-20 events over 2-5 days, deciding on extension depending on consistency.
157.when_to_use: When arranging and carrying out direct observation timing and length, when it is necessary to ensure the sample size suffices to show behavior-consequence relationships.
157.trigger: When there are only few samples, relationships are unstable, or high-frequency times and locations are not yet covered.

158.skill_name: Manipulating attention consequences to test causality
158.skill_description: Using experimental methods to systematically manipulate others' attention or gaining opportunities in the behavioral consequences, observing the problem behavior increase or decrease with the independent variable, to verify the causal relationship of socially-mediated positive reinforcement.
158.when_to_use: At the assessment stage with experimental conditions, when it is necessary to confirm whether relevant relationships are causal.
158.trigger: When observation and investigation suggest it may be maintained by attention, but causal evidence is still lacking and consequence manipulation is needed to test it.

185.skill_name: Interviewing the help-seeker and key informants
185.skill_description: Proactively identify and contact key informants such as the help-seeker and their parents and spouse, and conduct direct conversation to obtain first-hand information related to the problem behavior, laying the foundation for subsequently determining target behaviors and conducting functional analysis.
185.when_to_use: In the initial stage of problem functional analysis of behavior, when background and behavioral information related to the case needs to be quickly collected to carry out assessment.
185.trigger: When the help-seeker themselves or informed persons familiar with their behavior such as parents or spouse can be contacted and indicate willingness to provide information related to the problem behavior.

186.skill_name: Selecting and using appropriate assessment methods and tools
186.skill_description: According to the situation choose interviews, telephone interviews, questionnaires, and rating scales, prioritizing structured tools (such as motivation rating scales, functional assessment interview forms), to clarify the target behavior and explore the crux of the problem behavior.
186.when_to_use: When structured, systematic data collection is needed in the early assessment stage, or when multi-source information needs a unified framework for comparison and summary.
186.trigger: When the target behavior and the root of the problem need to be more clearly determined, and available channels and tools such as interviews, telephone, questionnaires or scales are at hand.

187.skill_name: Guides the respondent to provide specific events and focus on antecedents and consequences
187.skill_description: Explain at the opening of the interview and remind repeatedly during the process, requiring the interviewee to provide concrete situations and descriptions of observable behavior, avoiding subjective inference, and narrating around the antecedent events of the behavior's occurrence and the consequences that followed.
187.when_to_use: When conducting any form of investigative interview or questionnaire supplementation, when it is necessary to improve the observability and operability of information to serve functional analysis.
187.trigger: When the respondent answers with general evaluations, subjective interpretations, or skipping details, frequently using speculative phrasings such as 'feel, should, maybe'.

188.skill_name: Analyzing assessment data to form preliminary functional hypotheses
188.skill_description: Organize the relationship between the environmental events obtained from investigation and specific problem behaviors, analyze the association between behavior event characteristics and behavior increase or decrease, and propose preliminary hypotheses about behavior function, providing a basis for subsequent evaluation and treatment plans.
188.when_to_use: After completing one or more rounds of data collection, before formulating further observation plans or drafting intervention directions.
188.trigger: When a description containing the situation, antecedent events, the specific behavior and its consequences has been obtained, and clues appear that frequency or intensity varies with the situation.

189.skill_name: Cross-validate survey conclusions with observational methods
189.skill_description: Given that the investigation method relies on recall and is easily affected by forgetting and bias, arrange direct observation to verify key antecedents and consequences, integrating the two types of data to revise and refine the functional hypothesis, thereby improving the accuracy and credibility of the information.
189.when_to_use: When the information obtained from investigation is inconsistent, evidence is insufficient, or the functional hypothesis is not yet stable, needing further verification.
189.trigger: When different respondents' statements contradict each other, details are vague, or forgetting and bias are noticed as potentially affecting information accuracy.

159.skill_name: Determine the escape/avoidance function of the problem behavior
159.skill_description: Based on the functional analysis, judge whether the behavior is maintained by negative reinforcement given by others, that is, reinforced by escaping or avoiding aversive demands. Combined with the records of 'escape/avoidance' and 'the real behavioral consequences' in the functional assessment observation form, confirm whether the behavior takes terminating the demand as the main consequence.
159.when_to_use: In the initial functional analysis and direct observation data summary stage, used to form or verify behavior function hypotheses.
159.trigger: After the behavior occurs the individual leaves the task, pauses demands, or avoids homework by standing-punishment and the like; caregivers report 'making a fuss means not having to do it'.

160.skill_name: Survey interviews focusing on antecedents and consequences to identify the escape function
160.skill_description: In interviews, phone calls, or scale surveys, require the respondent to specifically describe antecedent events such as demands, difficult tasks, or interruptions occurring before the behavior, and whether a result of leaving the demand was obtained after the behavior. Emphasize objective events and consequences, avoid subjective inference, and focus on escape-related clues.
160.when_to_use: The indirect investigation stage of functional analysis, before forming preliminary conclusive statements.
160.trigger: The interviewee can recall concrete event chains such as 'acts up as soon as a task is assigned' and 'after acting up, the teacher lets them go out', but mostly uses subjective comments.

161.skill_name: Recording avoidance indicators with the functional assessment observation form
161.skill_description: During direct observation, record the time, problem behavior, and antecedent events, and under 'perceived function of the behavior' tick 'escape/avoidance'. Also record the 'actual behavioral consequences' in detail, checking whether the behavior consistently results in leaving a demand or termination of a task, to support a determination of escape function.
161.when_to_use: During the direct observation stage of functional analysis and baseline data collection.
161.trigger: When demands are made, difficult tasks are begun, or activities are interrupted, the problem behavior occurs frequently, and after the behavior the client gains leaving the setting or stopping the task.

162.skill_name: Reviewing consequences to avoid unintentionally reinforcing escape
162.skill_description: Based on the 'actual behavioral consequences' in the observation table, examine whether practices such as isolation, leaving the room, and pausing tasks let the problem behavior obtain an escape outcome; if this pattern is found, correct the strategy in time to prevent escape being used as reinforcement, causing the problem behavior to be maintained or worsen.
162.when_to_use: When observation data interpretation, plan drafting, or execution is frustrated and needs revision.
162.trigger: Records show that after episodes the person is often taken away from demand situations or isolated, yet the problem behavior frequency does not decrease but increases.

163.skill_name: When avoidance is maintained, avoid removing demand situations
163.skill_description: When the conclusive statement shows the problem behavior is maintained by escaping demands, when formulating and executing the plan do not adopt the approach of 'letting them leave the demand situation' at the moment the behavior appears, avoiding using demand removal as a consequence, blocking the provision of negative reinforcement at the source.
163.when_to_use: When the behavior therapy plan is formulated and on-site coping strategies are implemented.
163.trigger: When functional assessment identifies 'escaping demands' as the maintaining function, and the implementer tends to adopt the handling of 'go out to calm down first / do not do it first'.

164.skill_name: Adjust immediate antecedent events to weaken escape motivation
164.skill_description: Follow the principle of 'changing immediate antecedent events', adjust task difficulty, length, activity arrangement, or attention level, reduce the aversiveness of demands, break the connection between problem behavior and antecedent events, thereby weakening the reinforcing value of escape.
164.when_to_use: Scheme design and situation modification stage, when needing to preventively reduce the probability of episodes.
164.trigger: Observation shows that problem behavior increases markedly in demand situations of high difficulty, long duration, or that are interrupted.

165.skill_name: Motivational analysis evaluating the value of escape reinforcement
165.skill_description: Systematically assess which demands or activities are aversive stimuli for the person and how high the reinforcement value of escaping these stimuli is, thereby selecting effective reinforcers and replacement strategies, supporting the establishment of new responses and reducing escape maintenance.
165.when_to_use: In the motivational-assessment stage of functional analysis, providing a basis for plan materials and reinforcement arrangement.
165.trigger: The person strongly resists a specific activity, often escapes through complaining or disruption, and subjectively experiences 'ease / relief'.

166.skill_name: Experimentally manipulate task variables to verify the escape function
166.skill_description: Systematically manipulate independent variables such as task difficulty, length, attention level, or opportunities to choose activities, observe whether the problem behavior changes systematically with the manipulation, so as to establish a causal link of demand — behavior — consequence, verify escape/avoidance as the maintaining function, and exclude extra variables.
166.when_to_use: When indirect and direct data are insufficient or conclusions are doubtful, needing causal verification.
166.trigger: Existing data are correlational but not causal; professional conditions exist to implement control and supervision for functional experiments.

167.skill_name: Increasing the relative reinforcement value of appropriate behavior
167.skill_description: When testing and adjusting behavioral consequences, ensure that the reinforcement provided for appropriate behavior is equal to or greater than the reinforcement the problem behavior obtains through escape, increasing the relative benefit of the replacement behavior and weakening the function of problem behavior aimed at escape.
167.when_to_use: When setting up and optimizing the reinforcement system, advancing alternative-behavior teaching and maintenance.
167.trigger: The individual often gains strong reinforcement such as 'exemption/reduced burden' through problem behavior, while desired behavior lacks timely and effective reinforcement.

226.skill_name: Clarifying and defining the behavior-change tasks of family and teachers
226.skill_description: In the plan, prioritizing the design of specific behaviors that supporters such as family/teachers need to change in different situations, and clearly and operably defining their target responses, to facilitate correction of the person's problem behavior.
226.when_to_use: In the stage of establishing a behavioral treatment plan, needing to translate intervention intent into an executable checklist, clarifying who does what where.
226.trigger: Functional assessment and observational data show that surrounding people's reactions affect the maintenance of problem behavior, requiring external behavior change to cooperate with intervention.

227.skill_name: Plan systematic adjustments to environment and task structure
227.skill_description: List in the plan the environmental-level modifications: change the physical environment, adjust the curriculum, replace reinforcers / punishers, change teaching methods, making the environment support appropriate behavior and reduce the occurrence of problem behavior.
227.when_to_use: When designing the plan, it is found that change is hard to maintain by individual internal effort alone, and the environment and task structure need to be optimized to improve results.
227.trigger: Assessment or observation suggests the physical environment, course arrangements, or teaching methods restrict appropriate behavior or maintain the problem behavior.

228.skill_name: Structuring functional-assessment conclusions and formulating dos and don'ts
228.skill_description: Structuring the conclusive statements from functional assessment into the plan, clarifying functionally desirable and prohibited strategies, as the basis and boundary for all intervention choices.
228.when_to_use: After completing the functional assessment and entering plan formulation and decision-making, when conclusions need to be converted into concrete operational guidelines.
228.trigger: When the conclusive statement already points to a function (e.g. self-stimulation or escaping demands), needing to accordingly avoid practices that reinforce the problem function and clarify alternative strategies.

229.skill_name: Check the consistency of the plan with behavioral principles
229.skill_description: Checking the proposed plan for behavioral-principle consistency, ensuring the intervention follows basic learning principles, using environment and consequences to support appropriate behavior and reduce problem behavior.
229.when_to_use: At the quality-control stage before the plan is finalized, when it is necessary to verify that technique choices match learning principles.
229.trigger: When the draft plan shows signs inconsistent with learning principles, such as over-relying on punishment, neglecting reinforcement arrangement, or lacking consequence management.

230.skill_name: Assessing and matching the implementer's capabilities, resources, and values
230.skill_description: Examining the match between the plan and the implementer's ability, resources and values, ensuring it is easy to execute in natural situations, and adjusting to obtain short-term visible reinforcement results to improve compliance.
230.when_to_use: The plan design and pre-implementation assessment stage, when it is necessary to confirm implementation feasibility and motivational basis.
230.trigger: When the implementer expresses difficulty/resistance or resources are limited, or intervention demands exceed what the existing environment and ability can bear.

231.skill_description: Based on the concluding statement, establishing appropriate behavior functionally equivalent to the problem behavior, enabling the individual to obtain the same function with the new behavior, replacing the problem behavior at the source.
231.when_to_use: When the function is clear but feasible alternative paths are lacking, the goal focuses on the acquisition and maintenance of new behavior.
231.trigger: Assessment shows the problem behavior is maintained by a specific function, while the existing plan focuses only on consequence management and lacks teaching of alternative behaviors.

232.skill_name: Choosing interventions that leave problem behavior no room to function
232.skill_description: Adding strategies to the plan that make problem behavior unable to achieve its function again, so its consequences no longer satisfy the existing functional needs, weakening problem behavior at the functional level.
232.when_to_use: Replacement behavior teaching in parallel, needing to weaken the utility of the old behavior through functional-level consequence design.
232.trigger: Conclusive statements clearly maintain consequences; the link between the problem behavior and its function can be cut by adjusting the consequence path.

233.skill_name: Adjust distal setting events to reduce interference
233.skill_description: Deeply sorting out and changing long-term situational events so they no longer hinder the change of problem behavior, providing stable background support for subsequent antecedent and consequence interventions.
233.when_to_use: When broad or persistent background conditions are found to affect intervention effectiveness, needing to first optimize situational events.
233.trigger: When data show problem behavior occurs more easily under specific background conditions or intervention effects are unstable, suggesting situational events are at play.

234.skill_name: Change immediate antecedent events to break the link
234.skill_description: Adjusting already-identified immediate antecedent events (e.g. demands, difficult tasks, interruptions), weakening their functional link with problem behavior to reduce occurrence.
234.when_to_use: When observation records have clarified the antecedent events triggering the problem behavior, needing to modify them from the antecedent end.
234.trigger: When antecedent-event patterns are clear in functional data, and problem behavior appears highly consistently under specific triggers.

235.skill_name: Develop teaching strategies for expectations and alternative behaviors
235.skill_description: In the plan, list the teaching steps and methods for acquiring desired and alternative behaviors, so that new behaviors are learned to replace old ones, in preference to merely suppressing problem behaviors.
235.when_to_use: When the plan shows too much suppression and insufficient skill acquisition, needing to supplement the teaching path.
235.trigger: When the plan or assessment suggests the person lacks the appropriate skills to complete tasks, or the intervention only emphasizes reducing problem behavior.

236.skill_name: Checking and adjusting the consequence-reinforcement balance
236.skill_description: Systematically checking the reinforcement obtained by problem and appropriate behaviors, adjusting consequences so that reinforcement for appropriate behavior equals or exceeds that for problem behavior, and considering that individual preferences change over time, updating reinforcers promptly.
236.when_to_use: In the consequence-management design and review stage, needing to ensure the reinforcement arrangement supports the maintenance and generalization of target behavior.
236.trigger: When data show problem behavior is reinforced by escaping aversives or gaining attention, or appropriate behavior lacks effective and sufficient reinforcement.

173.skill_name: Identifying the functional pattern of sensory negative reinforcement
173.skill_description: Based on the functional definition, identifying situations where after the behavior occurs negative stimuli are automatically reduced or eliminated, not depending on others' consequences; combined with examples such as actively closing windows in cold weather, judging it as sensory negative reinforcement.
173.when_to_use: In initial functional analysis and early observation stages, when needing to define whether problem behavior is maintained by sensory negative reinforcement, especially when data are limited and a functional hypothesis must first be made.
173.trigger: When the client, in an aversive stimulus situation, immediately shows a certain behavior, and the stimulus then weakens or disappears; such as proactively closing the window when the weather is cold and the cold wind is then blocked.

174.skill_name: Uses an assessment observation form to record escape-avoidance functions and consequences
174.skill_description: Using the functional assessment observation form, recording time, context, antecedent events, and in the escape/avoidance and real behavioral consequence columns marking whether the behavior was negatively reinforced by automatically reducing negative stimuli, providing evidence for functional judgment.
174.when_to_use: In the direct-observation stage, used to verify the functional hypothesis formed by indirect investigation, when needing to clarify whether a negative-reinforcement (escape/avoidance) function exists.
174.trigger: It is observed that the problem behavior frequently appears after specific antecedent events, and negative stimuli subsequently decrease or disappear; or indirect investigation suggests the possibility of escape/avoidance.

175.skill_name: Enhancing alternative-behavior reinforcement by the functional-equivalence principle
175.skill_description: According to the principle of functional equivalence, establish appropriate behaviors functionally equivalent to the problem behavior, and review the consequence arrangements, ensuring the reinforcement the appropriate behavior obtains is equal to or greater than the effect of the problem behavior's automatic reduction of aversive stimulation.
175.when_to_use: In the stage of establishing a behavioral treatment plan, when functional-assessment conclusions have been formed and reinforcement strategies need to be selected and arranged.
175.trigger: When the conclusive statement shows problem behavior is maintained by escape/avoidance function, or existing consequence arrangements keep it occurring, needing intervention through consequence and reinforcement resetting.

176.skill_name: Changing immediate antecedent events to weaken negative reinforcement
176.skill_description: According to observation data, adjust the antecedent events immediately adjacent to the problem behavior, decoupling them from the conditions that bring relief of aversive stimulation, weakening the likelihood of the problem behavior maintained by sensory negative reinforcement occurring in that situation.
176.when_to_use: Before and after refining and implementing the intervention plan, when certain immediate antecedent events are found consistently correlated with problem behavior, needing adjustment at the situational level.
176.trigger: The functional assessment observation form shows that the problem behavior often occurs in specific immediate antecedent events, and negative stimuli decrease along with it; for example, related behaviors are more likely to appear in cold situations.

177.skill_name: Initially distinguishing behavioral insufficiency or behavioral excess
177.skill_description: Comprehensively judge the nature of the problem behavior according to four clues: social norms, impairment of life functioning, the help-seeker's subjective distress, and evaluations by people around, taking into account behavioral complexity and situational context, avoiding one-sided diagnosis.
177.when_to_use: In the starting stage of problem functional analysis of behavior, used to clarify the nature and boundaries of the client's problem, determining the focus for subsequent observation and recording.
177.trigger: The client is unsure whether their behavior is 'excessive/not enough'; reports life impairment or marked distress; surrounding people have divergent evaluations of their behavior.

178.skill_name: Analyzes the situations, frequency, intensity, and duration of problem behavior occurrence
178.skill_description: Systematically reviewing the frequency, intensity, duration and influencing factors of behavior in different situations, identifying antecedent or concurrent visible/invisible stimuli, recording in which specific situations the count increases or decreases.
178.when_to_use: Used after the target behavior has been determined and before an observation and recording plan is made, to depict behavior-situation associations and measurement dimensions.
178.trigger: The client describes the behavior as more frequent or stronger at specific times/places/tasks; mentions change clues such as 'when encountering a certain stimulus' 'lasts very long/very short'.

179.skill_name: Evaluating the reinforcing role of aversive and pleasant stimuli
179.skill_description: Identifying pleasant or aversive stimuli with unique reinforcing potency for the help-seeker, analyzing their role in maintaining problem behavior, and laying the foundation for subsequently selecting effective reinforcers to establish new responses.
179.when_to_use: In functional analysis when the maintaining mechanism needs interpretation, or before preparing to design a reinforcement plan and teach alternative behaviors.
179.trigger: The client mentions acquisition consequences such as 'liking/enjoying/comfortable/being noticed', or avoidance consequences such as 'wanting to avoid/very uncomfortable/under great pressure'; talks about motivations of reward or avoiding punishment.

180.skill_name: Examines developmental factors such as maturation, illness, and social change
180.skill_description: Assess the impact of maturation, illness and changes in the social environment on behavioral performance, calibrate it in combination with the consistency of behavior with social conventions, and avoid misjudging developmental limitations as purely functional problems.
180.when_to_use: When clues appear of developmental-stage, health-status, or social-environment changes, needing to examine these developmental factors' limiting or triggering roles on behavior.
180.trigger: Situations where the client reports recent illness, entering a new school stage / position, moving, or important relationship changes after which behavior changed accordingly.

181.skill_name: Assess the help-seeker's self-control efforts and outcomes
181.skill_description: Understanding the strategies the help-seeker has tried to control or change the problem behavior, the investment and outcomes, evaluating their self-regulation ability and available resources, providing a basis for intervention difficulty and path selection.
181.when_to_use: In functional analysis when the past change history needs evaluation, judging self-help ability and intervention feasibility.
181.trigger: The client mentions efforts such as 'tried to control/restrain/quit/adjust routines', or describes outcomes such as briefly effective but recurring, or completely ineffective.

182.skill_name: Assesses the attitudes of the help-seeker and people around toward the problem behavior
182.skill_description: Collect the attitudes of approval or opposition toward the behavior from the help-seeker and significant others, analyze their role in maintaining or inhibiting the behavior, and clarify the social consequences and communication focus that need adjustment.
182.when_to_use: When planning systematic intervention, before mobilizing supporters such as family/teachers to cooperate, used to grasp the direction of social consequences.
182.trigger: The client relays things like 'family thinks it is not a problem / will indulge / will criticize / firmly opposes'; attention, blame, or indulgence given by others affects the behavior.

183.skill_name: Assessing the influence of the physical environment on behavior
183.skill_description: Taking stock of how physical-environment elements such as residence, learning and work limit or facilitate behavior, identifying adjustable environmental details, such as the influence of space, distance, facilities on behavior opportunities.
183.when_to_use: Before drafting an intervention, when needing to confirm that behavior occurrence probability and maintaining conditions can be influenced through environmental modification.
183.trigger: The client describes physical-environment constraints such as 'living remotely / cramped space / inconvenient commute / lacking facilities / noise or temperature effects'.

184.skill_name: Integrate seven aspects of information into a conclusive statement
184.skill_description: Integrate evidence on behavior nature, situational measurement, motivational reinforcement, developmental factors, self-control, social attitudes, and physical environment, clarify key antecedent events and consequences, and form an operable conclusive statement to guide the plan.
184.when_to_use: After completing information gathering, entering the stage of formulating a behavioral treatment plan, when the functional-assessment conclusions need to be used to select techniques and avoid mistaken interventions.
184.trigger: Multi-source data obtained from investigation and observation but judgments are scattered; the team or family needs a clear functional hypothesis to decide the intervention path.

246.skill_name: Non-interventional direct observation with sequential recording
246.skill_description: The observer does not intervene in the observed person's activities, observes objectively, and records item by item in the order events occur, then conducts comprehensive analysis, meeting the scientific-observation requirements of purposefulness, planning and systematicity.
246.when_to_use: In the functional assessment and behavior observation stage, when objective data need to be obtained directly to verify or clarify conclusions formed by indirect investigation.
246.trigger: Indirect-investigation conclusions are vague or contradictory, or cannot provide useful data; on-site activities are proceeding naturally and conditions should not be manipulated.

247.skill_name: Select observers and obtain informed consent
247.skill_description: Selecting professionals or persons with fixed ties to the person in natural situations to perform observation; obtaining the consent of the person or guardian before starting, especially in observation situations where the person is unaware.
247.when_to_use: Used before formulating and launching functional assessment observation, to clarify who carries out observation and recording, ensuring the data are reliable and compliant.
247.trigger: Planning to conduct observation in natural situations such as school or home; arrangements involving minors or covert observation need consent secured.

248.skill_name: Determining the timing and location of observations
248.skill_description: Based on investigation data, gathering information on specific situations and different time periods, and deciding the actual observation time and place based on when and where the problem behavior occurs or not.
248.when_to_use: When arranging the observation plan, to increase the probability of capturing the target behavior and cover key situations and time periods.
248.trigger: Clues already show problem behavior is more (or less) likely at certain times or places, needing to compare performance across different situations.

249.skill_name: Setting observation length and coverage criteria
249.skill_description: Continuing observation until the behavior-environment relationship is clearly presented; generally recording the target behavior at least 15-20 times, collecting 2-5 days of data consecutively, deciding whether to extend based on consistency and clarity.
249.when_to_use: At the start of and during observation, used to decide how long to observe and when to extend it to ensure data sufficiency and stability.
249.trigger: The target behavior occurs too few times; the behavior-environment relationship appears inconsistent or unclear; initial data cover fewer than 2-5 days or fluctuate greatly.

250.skill_name: Use the functional assessment observation form for systematic recording
250.skill_description: Structured recording with the functional assessment observation form: subject and date, time and activity, problem behavior, antecedent events (including preset indicators/supplements/unknown), perceived function, real consequence, remarks and event tracking.
250.when_to_use: In the direct observation process, when behavior, situations, and consequences need to be recorded comprehensively and in a standardized way, providing a basis for subsequent correction plans.
250.trigger: Entering the formal observation and recording stage; key elements such as antecedent events, functional hypotheses, and actual consequences need to be captured simultaneously.

251.skill_name: Interpreting observation-form data to verify or revise conclusions
251.skill_description: Interpret the data in four steps: examine the frequency and co-occurrence of behaviors; check the associations between time periods and indicators; compare the perceived function with the actual consequences; on this basis confirm, revise, or abandon the prior conclusion and develop new statements.
251.when_to_use: Used after completing one round or several days of observation, when the observation data need to be turned into a usable functional conclusion to guide the correction plan.
251.trigger: When the form shows the behavior consistently occurring at specific times, or perceived function does not match real consequences, suggesting the hypothesis needs adjustment or refinement.

252.skill_name: Verify or replace indirect survey conclusions with direct observation
252.skill_description: When indirect-investigation data are limited or heavily biased, using systematic direct observation to verify and clarify conclusive statements; if investigation is useless, using direct-observation data as the basis for functional hypotheses.
252.when_to_use: In early functional assessment or when investigation results are insufficient to support decisions, ensuring the intervention is built on reliable observational data.
252.trigger: When interviews, questionnaires or scales lose accuracy due to forgetting or bias, failing to clarify the antecedent-consequence relationship with problem behavior.

190.skill_name: Recording behavioral events objectively in natural order without intervention
190.skill_description: In direct observation not intervening in the person's activities, objectively recording problem behavior, antecedent events and behavioral consequences in the natural order of occurrence, avoiding controlling conditions, to obtain real, usable first-hand data.
190.when_to_use: In the direct-observation stage of problem functional analysis of behavior, used to obtain objective event-chain data to support functional hypotheses.
190.trigger: When the client conducts daily activities in natural situations with the target behavior occurring or likely occurring, or when indirect-investigation data are insufficient to clarify antecedents and consequences.

191.skill_name: Select suitable observers and obtain necessary consent
191.skill_description: Designating professionals or persons with fixed ties to the person as observers; obtaining the consent of the person or their parents/guardians before conducting observation and recording, especially ensuring ethics and legality when unaware observation is involved.
191.when_to_use: At the planning and preparation stage before starting direct observation, when personnel and ethical permissions are clarified.
191.trigger: When planning to conduct observation in the person's natural environment with the observer not yet determined, or when unaware observation may be conducted requiring consent.

192.skill_name: Determining the timing and location of observations based on indirect investigation
192.skill_description: Based on indirect-investigation results such as interviews/scales, choosing time periods and situations where problem behavior is more or less likely to occur for observation, making the sample cover key activities and environments, improving data representativeness.
192.when_to_use: Before setting the direct observation schedule and locations, used to optimize observation arrangements and improve the hit rate.
192.trigger: When investigation data suggest specific times, places or activities are related or unrelated to problem behavior occurrence, needing to arrange observation accordingly.

193.skill_name: Determine observation length until the relationship is clear
193.skill_description: Continuously collect data until the behavior-environment relationship is clear; in practice ensure the target behavior occurs at least 15-20 times, record continuously for 2-5 days; decide whether to extend the observation according to behavior frequency and relationship consistency.
193.when_to_use: When carrying out direct observation and staged reviews, used to determine the sustained duration and whether to extend the observation.
193.trigger: When observational data do not yet show a stable, consistent relationship, or the target behavior occurs too few times, or observation days have not yet reached the recommended range.

194.skill_name: Use the functional assessment observation form to record key elements
194.skill_description: Record completely in the form the object and date, time course and activities, confirmed problem behavior, antecedent events, perceived behavioral function (gain/escape), actual behavioral consequences, comments/remarks, events and dates, and other information.
194.when_to_use: During each direct observation session, when event chains and functional cues need to be collected systematically and in a standardized way.
194.trigger: When starting an observation period, when time, behavior, antecedents, functional judgments, actual consequences, and remarks need to be recorded simultaneously.

195.skill_name: Marking Unknown when antecedents or consequences are unclear
195.skill_description: When the antecedent events or real consequences of the problem behavior cannot be determined, marking 'do not know/not clear' in the corresponding form columns, avoiding subjective inference, maintaining the objectivity and testability of records.
195.when_to_use: When filling in the observation form and key information is missing or hard to confirm, when record quality must be maintained.
195.trigger: When the target behavior is observed but its antecedents or consequences cannot yet be clarified, or clues contradict each other and cannot be judged.

196.skill_name: Recording the times and situations when problem behavior does not yet appear
196.skill_description: Recording in comments/remarks under which environments and times the problem behavior does not yet occur, incorporating the 'not yet occurred' pattern into the data base, to help define triggers and maintaining conditions, improving functional-analysis clues.
196.when_to_use: After completing each observation segment, when supplementing meaningful contextual information to enrich the analysis.
196.trigger: When continuous observation at certain times or situations yields no target behavior, forming a stable 'not yet occurred' pattern.

197.skill_name: Using cameras and video tools to assist observation
197.skill_description: Due to sensory-organ limitations, modern instruments such as cameras and video recorders can be used to assist recording, improving the objectivity, systematicity and repeatability of observation, and facilitating playback review of details afterwards.
197.when_to_use: When on-site recording may miss details or needs later review and training, as an auxiliary means to direct observation.
197.trigger: When behavior occurs rapidly or the situation is complex and noisy, and manual recording is hard to capture the event chain in time and completely.

198.skill_name: Reviewing data sufficiency per the observation form's interpretation principles
198.skill_description: According to the observation table principles, examine behavior frequency and co-occurrence, time consistency, and event relationships, compare the perceived function with the real consequences, and on this basis judge whether the conclusion holds and decide whether to revise the hypothesis or continue collecting data.
198.when_to_use: When summarizing direct observation data at a stage, judging whether 'clear relationship' has been reached, and adjusting the plan.
198.trigger: When after consecutive days of recording a pattern inconsistent with the original hypothesis appears, or a stable time/event-behavior correspondence has not yet formed.

212.skill_description: In direct observation not intervening in the participant's activities, recording behaviors and environmental cues item by item in the order events occur, recording only visible facts, making no subjective inferences or causal judgments, preserving raw sequential data for subsequent functional analysis.
212.when_to_use: Used in the direct observation stage of functional assessment, when on-site recording is carried out to build a data base for the problem behavior and environmental events.
212.trigger: When the subject begins activities in a natural situation and the target behavior and related environmental events appear successively in natural order.

213.skill_name: Recording the target and temporal context
213.skill_description: Fill in the observation form with the person observed, the date, and the start and end times, and record the situational characteristics and activities engaged in during the period, providing temporal and situational references for locating antecedent events and behaviors.
213.when_to_use: Used when establishing the recording framework for this segment at the start of each observation period, or when the situation and activity change significantly and the record needs updating.
213.trigger: When starting a new segment of observation, switching locations or activities, or when a new time period needs to be marked.

214.skill_description: In the 'behavior' column listing the target/problem behaviors defined during this observation period, using clear, objective, operable descriptions, ensuring different observers can consistently identify and record their occurrence.
214.when_to_use: Before starting recording, when the target behavior list is clarified, or during observation when the target behavior first appears and needs to be registered.
214.trigger: When any defined target behavior is observed, or when entries need to be established for subsequent frequency and characteristic recording.

215.skill_name: Recording antecedent events and potential indicators
215.skill_description: Based on potential indicators preset from indirect investigation (e.g. demands, difficult tasks, interruptions, lack of attention) recording antecedent events, and supplementing new indicators; if temporarily undeterminable, marking 'do not know/not clear' in the form.
215.when_to_use: Before or at the same time as each target behavior occurs, when situational clues that may trigger the behavior need to be captured.
215.trigger: Used when observable situational changes such as task demands, interrupted activities, or reduced attention from others appear before the target behavior.

216.skill_name: Labeling the felt function of behaviors
216.skill_description: In the 'perceived function of the behavior' column, preliminarily check options such as obtain or escape / avoidance, and supplements such as obtaining attention, special activities, and self-stimulation may be added, used to form a preliminary hypothesis of the maintaining function.
216.when_to_use: After recording the antecedent and the behavior, when possible functional tendencies need to be preliminarily labeled to guide subsequent analysis.
216.trigger: After the behavior occurs, when there is a clear tendency to seek attention/items or to escape demands or activities.

217.skill_name: Recording the true consequences of behavior
217.skill_description: Record truthfully the actual consequences after the problem behavior occurs (such as gaining attention, leaving the task, obtaining objects), to examine the consistency between the perceived function and the actual consequences and to provide further clues.
217.when_to_use: Immediately after each target behavior ends, when its accompanying environmental changes and others' reactions are recorded.
217.trigger: When observable consequences such as soothing, reprimanding, isolation, withdrawal of demands, or giving rewards appear after the target behavior.

218.skill_name: Filling in comments and not-yet-occurred information
218.skill_description: In the 'comments/remarks' column supplementing important explanations, including recording situations where problem behavior does not yet occur at certain times or environments; such 'not yet occurred' information is equally evaluatively meaningful.
218.when_to_use: When exceptions needing explanation, background information appear, or behavior is continuously not yet occurring in specific situations.
218.trigger: When behavior stably does not yet occur in certain times or scenarios, or form entries need additional clarification and supplementation.

219.skill_name: Tracking event numbers and cross-day records
219.skill_description: In the 'event and date' column numbering each problem-behavior event and marking dates, to count occurrences and conduct cross-period comparisons and tracking across different observation dates.
219.when_to_use: When it is necessary to integrate data from multiple or cross-day observations for frequency statistics and pattern comparison.
219.trigger: After completing a round of observation and preparing to summarize, or when conducting continuous observation across days requiring continuity of event tracking.

220.skill_description: Continuously record until the behavior-environment relationship is clearly presented; usually have the target behavior occur at least 15-20 times and collect data within 2-5 days, deciding whether to extend according to the consistency and clarity of the relationship.
220.when_to_use: When formulating and implementing the duration and frequency arrangements of the observation recording plan, ensuring the amount of data is sufficient to support analysis.
220.trigger: When the target behavior occurs too few times, the behavior-environment relationship is not yet clear, or data consistency is insufficient.

199.skill_name: Designating an observer and obtaining consent
199.skill_description: Selecting professionals or persons with fixed ties to the person's natural environment as observers, obtaining the consent of the person or their parents/guardians before starting observation, especially authorizing in advance when the person may be unaware of the observation arrangement.
199.when_to_use: In the direct observation preparation stage before the functional assessment observation form is started, put in place the observer selection and ethical compliance, ensuring the records are legal and valid.
199.trigger: When planning to conduct observation in the person's natural situation and they are a minor or guardian authorization is needed, or observation is to be conducted while they are unaware.

200.skill_name: Determining the timing and location of observations
200.skill_description: Based on indirect-investigation data, choosing the timing and locations where problem behavior is most likely or least likely to occur, covering key activity situations, to record the association between behavior and environmental events.
200.when_to_use: When formulating a direct-observation plan, preparing to use the functional assessment observation form, for locating high-value observation windows.
200.trigger: Indirect investigation suggests that a specific time period, location or activity is related to the problem behavior, or that the person frequently shows problem behavior in a certain type of activity.

201.skill_name: Determining observation length and data standards
201.skill_description: Continue collecting data until the relationship between behavior and environment is clear; at the practical level, ensure the target behavior occurs at least 15-20 times, lasting 2-5 days, and extend the observation when necessary according to consistency and clarity.
201.when_to_use: During planning or conducting direct observation, when ensuring functional inferences have sufficient data support.
201.trigger: When the behavior-environment relationship is not yet clear in initial observation, or the target behavior occurs too few times to support conclusive statements.

202.skill_name: Filling in the observation target and data date
202.skill_description: Accurately fill in the observation subject and the data-collection date in the header, to uniquely identify the observed person and that observation record, facilitating integration and tracking across periods.
202.when_to_use: Before each new observation batch begins and the functional assessment observation form is used for recording.
202.trigger: The person enters the natural activity situation of this observation day, preparing to start recording.

203.skill_name: Recording observation time and situational activities
203.skill_description: Recording the concrete observation course and start/end in the 'time' column, and describing the situational features and activities engaged in at the time, forming a restorable time-situation thread.
203.when_to_use: During direct observation, accompanying each segment of activity or situational change, updating the form at any time.
203.trigger: At the start of the observation phase or when activities or situations change, such as entering a task, rest, transition, or being interrupted.

204.skill_description: In the 'behavior' column listing the target problem behaviors confirmed during the observation period, distinguishing concurrently occurring different behaviors when necessary, providing a basis for subsequent frequency and functional judgments.
204.when_to_use: During the direct observation recording period, whenever the target behavior needs to be identified and counted.
204.trigger: When the target behavior defined by the prior investigation appears, or its clear behavioral manifestation is observed.

205.skill_name: Recording antecedent events and potential indicators
205.skill_description: In the 'antecedent events' column first filling key indicators confirmed in investigation (e.g. demands, difficult tasks, interruptions, lack of attention), and supplementing other newly discovered potential triggers; marking 'not clear' when unknown.
205.when_to_use: Before and after problem behavior occurs, when needing to locate the antecedent conditions related to it.
205.trigger: Situations such as demands being made, difficult tasks, activities being interrupted, or lack of attention appear, or new suspicious triggering factors are observed.

206.skill_name: Labeling the felt function of behaviors
206.skill_description: In the 'perceived behavioral function' column, based on observation, conjecture the most likely function, check the gain or escape direction and concrete results (such as obtaining attention, special items/activities, self-stimulation, escaping demands), with supplementation allowed.
206.when_to_use: After recording each problem-behavior incident, when a preliminary functional judgment of its purpose tendency is made.
206.trigger: The client's problem behavior is accompanied by cues of gaining attention/items or successfully escaping demands, needing functional-tendency annotation.

207.skill_name: Recording the true consequences of behavior
207.skill_description: In the 'true behavior consequences' column, record the consequences the problem behavior actually brings, used to check which consequences are consistently provided, and provide further clues for the potential maintaining function.
207.when_to_use: After the problem behavior occurs, when it is necessary to objectively record behavioral consequences to check against functional inferences.
207.trigger: Observable consequences followed the problem behavior, such as being isolated, gaining attention / items, leaving the task, or having demands changed.

208.skill_name: Filling in comments and noting not-yet-occurred situations
208.skill_description: In the 'comments/remarks' column supplementing observer explanations, especially recording situations where problem behavior does not yet occur in certain environments or times; such missing information is equally interpretively meaningful.
208.when_to_use: In occasions during form recording needing background explanation or emphasizing not-yet-occurred information.
208.trigger: When problem behavior is observed not yet occurring at specific times or situations, or records need interpretation and supplementation.

209.skill_name: Tracking event counts and cross-day records
209.skill_description: Using the 'event and date' column to track the count of problem-behavior events and marking the observation dates spanning these events, providing a basis for frequency statistics and comparison across different observation days.
209.when_to_use: When completing multi-day observation or needing to summarize event frequency, comparing different dates.
209.trigger: After accumulating multiple events, when the total count needs to be tallied, or a cross-date trend comparison analysis is done.

210.skill_name: Review the relationship between behavior frequency and temporal antecedents
210.skill_description: According to the interpretation principles, first examine which behaviors are occurring, their frequency, and co-occurrence, then examine whether they consistently appear at specific times, and the association between specific antecedent indicators and specific behaviors.
210.when_to_use: After enough entries are collected, when moving into data interpretation to discover temporal and antecedent-condition patterns.
210.trigger: Repeated time-period patterns or antecedent indicators appear in the table, or certain behaviors frequently co-occur within the same time window.

211.skill_name: Revise the conclusion statement against function and consequences
211.skill_description: Compare 'the function of the behavior as felt' against 'the actual consequences', confirm the latent function and the maintaining consequences; use this to judge whether the existing conclusive statements are correct, and revise or add new statements when necessary.
211.when_to_use: Before formulating or adjusting the behavioral treatment plan, when observation-form data need to be used to verify and revise the functional hypothesis.
211.trigger: When the perceived function does not match the recorded real consequence, or existing conclusions hardly interpret the observational data.

281.skill_name: Negotiating to determine systematic desensitization and overall goals
281.skill_description: After psychological assessment and diagnosis, negotiating with the client and jointly deciding to use systematic desensitization, letting relaxation replace anxiety, while clarifying overall counseling goals and implementation plans, to guide subsequent sessions and training.
281.when_to_use: Used when the initial assessment and diagnostic stage ends and it is necessary to transition from information gathering to treatment planning; the client cooperates and is willing to participate.
281.trigger: The client explicitly seeks help, becomes markedly anxious when talking about learning and exams, describes palpitations, sweating, restlessness, and expresses the wish to improve.

282.skill_name: Sets phased goals: positive cognition and relaxation training
282.skill_description: Based on the stage arrangement, clarifying two core goals for this stage: building positive cognition through sessions to enhance confidence, and learning and mastering relaxation skills through behavioral relaxation training.
282.when_to_use: At the very beginning of entering the counseling and treatment stage, when the overall goal needs to be refined into operable stage tasks.
282.trigger: The client self-reports decreased self-confidence, feels upset and restless when reviewing, tense and uneasy, and is able to participate in relaxation practice.

283.skill_name: Clarifying this session's goal: building an anxiety hierarchy
283.skill_description: After completing initial relaxation training, setting 'building an anxiety-event hierarchy' as the goal of the current session, helping the client construct anxiety hierarchies related to socializing and exams, preparing for desensitization.
283.when_to_use: At the third counseling session, when relaxation training has been conducted several times and it is time to enter the systematic-desensitization preparation stage.
